bib.title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction

question: What should be tested and monitored in a production ML system, and how much is enough to call it production-ready?
hypothesis: A scored rubric of 28 ML-specific tests, whose total is the minimum over four sections, gives teams a quantified, incentivising measure of production readiness and technical debt paydown.
contributions: A rubric of 28 actionable tests across four sections (data, model development, ML infrastructure, monitoring)
A scoring system (ML Test Score) with an interpretation table
Findings from applying the rubric in structured interviews with 36 Google teams

method.summary: Authors derive 28 assertion-style tests from experience with production ML systems at Google (ad click prediction, Sibyl), grouped in 4 sections of 7. The score gives half a point per manually run documented test and 1 per automated test, sums per section, and takes the minimum across sections. Applied in structured interviews with 36 Google teams.

limits: No numeric per-test adoption data in text (Fig 4 only); no analysis of whether higher scores predict fewer incidents.
Score interpretation calibrated on internal Google systems only; authors say it matched qualitative perceptions.
Min-aggregation lowers visibility of individual effort; effect on adoption 'remains to be seen'.
Rubric excludes generic software engineering practices and targets supervised, continuously trained, low-latency server-side systems.
TFX assessment was a hypothetical system, not real ones.
Tests are hard where labels are scarce or expensive (Model 4, Infra 4); image/audio teams found many Data tests inapplicable; heuristic-label systems need testing the rubric does not cover.
Promised open-source unit test framework not released in the paper; dated 2017 (pre-MLOps tooling).
practices: Write each test as an assertion and run it as frequently as possible; fix the system if it fails (Sec I).
Capture feature expectations in a schema and use it to check training and serving inputs (Data 1, Monitor 2).
Remove features with minimal predictive benefit; measure latency, RAM, upstream dependencies, instability (Data 2-3).
Code review and version-control every model specification (Model 1).
Measure offline/online metric relationship via small A/B with an intentionally degraded model (Model 2).
Measure staleness impact with A/B on older models to get an age-vs-quality curve (Model 4).
Compare against a simple baseline model regularly (Model 5).
Add slice-based release thresholds, absolute and incremental (Model 6).
Unit test a model spec with random data and a single gradient step; avoid golden tests (Infra 2).
Run automated full-pipeline integration tests continuously and per release (Infra 3).
Validate model quality before serving with loose thresholds vs validation set and tight thresholds vs previous version (Infra 4).
Canary new models on a small traffic fraction, and practise rollback routinely (Infra 6-7).
Monitor dependencies, input invariants, training/serving skew, model age, NaNs/infs, compute performance, and prediction quality including bias (Monitor 1-7).
